# 0052: Scope is a boundary, not a roster, so a new release arrives without an edit

Status: accepted, 2026-09-29.
Refines [0051](0051-long-context-is-a-tier-priced-per-call-and-records-are-curated.md) (records are curated): the watched families become a shape and a generation floor.
A Claude tier becomes any word in the tier position.
Keeps [0007](0007-unpriced-model-aborts-before-spend.md)'s refusal for an ID whose shape is new.
It leaves [0049](0049-effort-is-the-third-matrix-axis.md)'s closed effort vocabulary closed.
The rule here is for what a provider will add, not for what a CLI accepts.

## Context

The first curator scoped OpenAI with an enumerated set, `families={"gpt-5.6", "gpt-6"}`, and matched only IDs that began with one of those names.
The day OpenAI ships `gpt-7`, the curator would not see it.
There would be not an error, not a report, just a model absent from every record from then on.
A sweep that names it stops at collection as unpriced.
The Claude grammar had the same flaw in a louder form.
Its tier alternation (`opus|sonnet|haiku|fable|mythos`) would make a new tier an unparsable ID, stopping every curation until someone edited the list.

Both lists described the releases that existed when they were written.
Neither described what the scope was for: every current generation of OpenAI's `gpt-` line, and every Claude tier.

## Decision

**A scope is a shape plus a floor.** A watch owns every first-party ID of its provider that matches its shape and whose generation is at or above its floor.
For OpenAI the shape is `gpt-<number>...` and the floor is `5.6`.
The generation is compared numerically (`5.10` is above `5.6`, and `10` is above `6`).
So `gpt-6`, `gpt-7` and `gpt-7.1` are in scope as they appear.
A word after `gpt-` is a sub-line (`gpt-image`, `gpt-realtime`) and is outside the shape.
A generation below the floor is outside the boundary.
Neither is an error: they were never in scope.

**A vocabulary slot is a pattern, not a list.** Where a grammar has a slot providers fill with new names, the slot accepts any word of the right form.
A Claude tier is any lowercase word in the tier position, so a new tier is curated with no edit.

**A new shape still stops.** Inside the boundary, an ID the grammar cannot parse stops the run and names the ID (ADR 0007).
Examples are a dated first-party snapshot the grammar does not describe, or a suffix nobody has seen.
The boundary decides what is in scope; the grammar decides whether we understand it.
Only the second may block curation.

**Closed vocabularies stay closed where an open one is the bug.** ADR 0049 closes the effort vocabulary because a CLI accepts any rung and silently bills its default.
That is a vocabulary the plugin sends; this record is about names the plugin receives.
The test for which applies:
- if an unknown value would be silently misused, close the list
- if a new value would be silently ignored, name the boundary

## Consequences

`gpt-7` appears in the next curated record on the day LiteLLM lists it.
A changed report names it under `added`, so a reviewer sees the scope grow rather than discovering it did not.
Narrowing scope is now an explicit edit of a floor or a shape, not the omission of a name.
The curator's tests pin the boundary with releases that do not exist yet (`gpt-7`, `gpt-10-sol`, `claude-nova-6`).
So a regression to a roster fails a test.

## Lens

Name the boundary, not today's members.
A list of what exists now is correct on the day it is written and silently wrong on the next release.
A rule for what belongs keeps being right.
The only thing that should stop it is a shape nobody has seen.
